 Rubio urges Cubans to work with CIA 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—United States (US) Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday called for Cubans to make “discreet” contact with the American intelligence services as Washington seeks to force an end to the island’s communist government.

For months, President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have openly hinted at a military intervention or takeover of Cuba, ramping up economic, political and legal pressure on the country.

“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time,” Rubio said on social media.

“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”

The unusual post appeared to confirm that the CIA is currently active in Cuba after a long history of covert operations including backing the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961.

Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida earlier Friday, underlined his ambitions to impose regime change in Cuba.

“Those beautiful (US military) ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast,” he said. “They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez quickly dismissed Trump’s threats.

“Our coastline is full of beautiful beaches, but there are also razor-sharp limestone spikes, an inhospitable environment for those who make it to our shores with hostile purposes and lust for domination,” he posted.

– Energy blockade –

In the latest US move against the Cuban leadership, Florida’s top prosecutor this week announced an arrest warrant for former president Raul Castro on state murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year.

Castro, 95, is wanted on murder charges connected to the 1996 shooting down of two civilian aircraft from “Brothers to the Rescue,” an organization assisting Cubans fleeing to the US state by sea.

Castro, brother of the late revolutionary leader and US nemesis Fidel Castro, was indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May.

Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action that toppled Venezuela’s then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities.

Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has “no legal basis” and was an attempt “to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba.”

Washington also imposed a de facto energy blockade on Cuba in January, threatening to sanction any country that supplies fuel to the island of 9.4 million people.

news.title: Indian Americans in Michigan courted as Trump heads to Port Huron
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 24 (IANS) Michigan’s Indian American community, the largest Asian group in a state that could decide control of Congress, is being courted by Asian American political groups in the closing days of the midterm campaign, as President Donald Trump prepares to rally supporters in Port Huron on Sunday. Trump is scheduled to speak at McMorran Place in Port Huron on Sunday, according to the White House schedule, his third rally in three days after Fort Myers, Florida, on Friday and Perry, Georgia, on Saturday. The AAPI Victory Fund, a super PAC that backs Asian American candidates and voters, held a reception at the Godfrey Hotel in Detroit on October 17 attended by Senator Elissa Slotkin and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic candidate for governor, according to The Oakland Post, Oakland University’s student newspaper. “We established a super PAC, but that was a very explicit recognition,” the group’s president, Linh Nguyen, told the paper. “There was not enough political money that’s actually backing and supporting Asian voters and then Asian candidates.” Nguyen said states such as Michigan and Georgia, with large Asian American populations and a history as battlegrounds, had become increasingly important to the group’s organising. “We can be voting for people like Abdul El-Sayed and be proud of doing that,” Nguyen said, referring to the Democratic Senate candidate. The group’s Michigan endorsements include El-Sayed, Benson, Lieutenant Governor Garlin Gilchrist II and Indian American state legislator Ranjeev Puri. Indian Americans number about 138,644 in Michigan, the largest Asian ethnic group in the state, according to an AAPI Data fact sheet. The state has about 123,545 eligible Asian American voters. Michigan’s Indian American population is concentrated in Oakland County suburbs such as Troy, Novi, Canton and Farmington Hills, which fall in or near competitive House districts. The state’s only Indian American member of Congress, Democrat Shri Thanedar, represents the Detroit-based 13th District. Port Huron, in St. Clair County, lies in a Republican-leaning part of the state’s Thumb region. Indian American voters have leaned Democratic in recent elections, but Republicans have made gains with some immigrant communities. Both parties are competing this cycle against a backdrop of tighter H-1B visa rules and a surge in anti-Indian rhetoric online. Michigan voters will choose a governor, a US senator and all 13 House members on November 3.

news.title: Cuba mocks US ‘desperation’ after Rubio urges Cubans to work with CIA
news.text:
HAVANA: Cuba on Friday mocked what it called US “desperation” after Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change to establish discreet ties with the CIA, as President Donald Trump renewed suggestions of possible US military intervention on the communist-run island.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.

“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste,” he added.

Rubio made his appeal in a social media post, urging Cubans dissatisfied with their government to seize what he described as an opportunity for change.

“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time,” Rubio wrote, citing what he called failed promises, corruption and the privileged lives of a few.

He encouraged them to pursue change through a “discreet partnership with the CIA.”

The agency subsequently posted a Spanish-language video on X explaining how people could submit information. It advised potential sources to visit an official US installation in person if they could do so safely, or to use a secure internet connection, a private browser and a disposable email account when contacting the agency online.

The public appeal came hours after Trump revived the prospect of military intervention in Cuba during a rally in Florida.

Trump said US warships returning from the war with Iran could stop off the Cuban coast before he sent Rubio to “finish up the deal.”

“Those beautiful (US military) ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast,” Trump said. “They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Trump has repeatedly raised the prospect of action against Cuba, while his administration has increased economic and political pressure on the island.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez dismissed the president’s remarks, warning that the country’s coastline would pose dangers to anyone arriving with hostile intentions.

“Our coastline is full of beautiful beaches, but there are also razor-sharp limestone spikes, an inhospitable environment for those who make it to our shores with hostile purposes and lust for domination,” Rodriguez wrote on X.

Pressure mounts on Havana

Washington has pursued a tougher approach toward Cuba as efforts to improve relations have stalled. The administration has imposed additional sanctions and maintained a de facto energy blockade introduced in January, threatening penalties against countries supplying fuel to the island of about 9.4 million people.

The latest escalation also comes amid legal action against former Cuban President Raul Castro, 95. Florida’s top prosecutor announced an arrest warrant this week on state murder charges connected to the 1996 shooting down of two civilian aircraft operated by Brothers to the Rescue, an organization that assisted Cubans fleeing to the United States.

Castro was also indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May. The Cuban government has rejected the federal case, with President Miguel Diaz-Canel calling it legally unfounded and accusing Washington of seeking to justify military aggression.

Trump previously cited US criminal charges against Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro as part of the justification for the operation that toppled him. Maduro was a close ally of Havana.

The United States and Cuba have held talks in recent months, but Washington has expressed dissatisfaction with their progress. Trump has portrayed Cuba as a potential target for stronger action after the conflict with Iran, while Rubio has questioned whether a diplomatic settlement is possible under the island’s current leadership.

Cuba has been grappling with a prolonged economic and energy crisis, marked by power outages, shortages, inflation and emigration. The US embargo, in place for decades, remains a central source of tension between the two countries.

news.title: DOJ demands that some California counties set aside alleged noncitizen ballots
news.text: Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press.The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Trump's Justice Department, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.Earlier this month, the federal government targeted L.A. County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of more than 20,000 people who it alleges are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.The Trump administration on Friday asked the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.Now, according to the L.A. County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48-hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified."Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including Social Security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county.California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.The letters on Friday came on the heels of a statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date. "This is NOT A DRILL: Donald Trump and Todd Blanche are trying to interfere in California elections," Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said in a statement Friday. "Trump's DOJ has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud. They've admitted that the data they point to is inaccurate and unreliable. No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere."
news.summary: Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens.
news.author: The Associated Press

Minister of Works, David Umahi, says the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway may not be completed if President Bola Tinubu fails to secure a second term in 2027.

Umahi disclosed this on Friday while speaking in an exclusive interview on Arise Television.

According to him, the 750-kilometre road is a personal initiative of President Tinubu and needs continuity to be fully delivered, saying that only Tinubu’s return can guarantee the completion of the project and other legacy roads across the country.

The former Ebonyi State governor also dismissed reports that the coastal highway had been abandoned for the East-West Road.

Russia indicated its readiness to resume the talks, which have been at a standstill since the beginning of the year, following a meeting this week in Saint Petersburg between President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff.

The next round of talks towards ending the Ukraine war, which is grinding through its fifth year, are “planned for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi”, and “will take place in a trilateral format”, Peskov told reporters.

The announcement came amid intensified diplomatic efforts by US President Donald Trump’s administration, with Witkoff first meeting on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo, before meeting with Putin on Wednesday.

news.title: 'This is not normal': Feds demand California counties set aside 'likely' noncitizen ballots
news.text: The U.S. Justice Department expanded its efforts to intervene in California's ongoing election Friday, sending letters to more than a dozen county elections offices statewide with demands that they segregate ballots from voters the Trump administration believes are noncitizens. The letters — which give officials 48 hours to act and threaten them with criminal punishments if they refuse — follow similar correspondence the Justice Department sent last week to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Dean Logan, head of the L.A. County registrar’s office, calling for some 20,000 ballots statewide be set aside and left uncounted until state and local officials can prove that the voters are citizens. When Weber and Logan balked, the Justice Department promptly sued them and the state in a case currently pending in federal court. The California officials have contended the Justice Department's efforts are illegal. The new letters, first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle, follow previous threats from Justice Department officials and President Trump warning that local California elections officials could face criminal prosecution for being “aiders and abettors to a federal crime" if they tabulate votes from the "likely noncitizens" the administration has flagged. First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, wrote Friday evening on X that "California does not verify citizenship status. We did the work for them. We obtained the registered voter list and told them who we believe are noncitizens on their rolls." Essayli wrote that "knowingly processing noncitizen ballots is a federal crime," and said authorities "will hold election officials accountable. No one is above the law." The Justice Department did not respond to an inquiry from The Times. California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta's office declined to comment. Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said that she personally knew of 15 counties that received a letter, and had "heard that there are others." "From what I’ve been able to gather, most counties if not all of the counties are doing what I’m doing: Sat down with our counsel, went over everything," Webber said. Webber said two people with Justice Department credentials showed up at her office Friday and handed her a manila envelope with the letter inside demanding she comply within 48 hours to determine the citizenship of 81 people in her county. "I can’t tell you anything other than I’m looking at it and doing my due diligence," she said. "This is not normal protocol for us." Kristin Connelly, head of the Contra Costa County registrar's office, said she was also among those who received a letter. She said she had not yet responded as of late Friday, but was in contact with her county counsel and "colleagues around the state who received similar letters today." "The non-partisan Contra Costa County Elections Division administers elections according to all state and federal election laws, as well as the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution of the State of California. Our work is observable," Connelly said. "This threat is not helpful and is intended to intimidate." The letter she received, from U.S. Atty. Craig Missakian, was full of threats of criminal punishment for tabulating votes from individuals whom the county is "on actual notice" may not be U.S. citizens. Missakian, the top federal prosecutor in the Northern District of California, wrote that he was providing Connelly with a "subset" of "407 likely aliens" from the broader statewide list of 20,000 voters, and demanded that Connelly commit within 48 hours to working with Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security officials to identify who among those 407 "is a citizen and who is not." "That means sending us the nonpublic information associated with each suspected alien's registration, which includes everything in your possession from the following: a social security number, a copy of a state ID or driver's license or the information that appears on it, a copy of the voter registration application supporting the registration, and a copy or list of documents that were presented by the registrant at the time the person registered to vote or obtained their driver's license if registered as part of motor voter," Missakian wrote. He also wrote that he was reaching out by letter "to make unmistakably clear the legal implications of continuing to send vote-by-mail ballots to those people on the list or tabulating ballots cast by them until citizenship can be verified." The Justice Department previously sued California for its voter records. A federal judge rejected the lawsuit, calling the demands a threat to democracy. The Justice Department has also lost similar cases demanding voter rolls in dozens of other states. California Sen. Alex Padilla said in a statement Friday that, "Donald Trump and Todd Blanche are trying to interfere in California elections." Padilla, the ranking Democrat on the U.S. Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which has oversight over federal elections, added: No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere." Padilla told local election officials, "We have your back." “The Trump administration is afraid and desperate," he said. "Their attempts to take over our elections will fail." The Justice Department has received some records by subpoenaing state and county officials for the records of specific voters. The letters were a topic of discussion among members of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials Friday, with officials working on how to respond. Logan, L.A. County's top elections official, sent an email to fellow association members saying he had seen a copy of the letter to some counties — which he condemned as misrepresenting facts and threatening elections officials "twelve days before the election" through a "posture of intimidation." Logan called the 48-hour deadline for responses "unenforceable," and noted that the Justice Department was "demanding individual level data from the named counties similar to what it has previously only obtained through subpoenas." Logan's office has also said that an initial review it conducted of a subset of the 20,000 voters the Justice Department initially flagged found many were born in the U.S., many weren't actually registered and many had never voted.
news.summary: The Justice Department sent letters to more than a dozen county elections offices statewide Friday demanding they segregate ballots from voters the Trump administration believes are not U.S. citizens.
news.author: Brittny Mejia,Kevin Rector

news.title: Iran's Plots To Assassinate American Diplomats Abroad At ‘Advanced Stages’, US Intel Warns: Report
news.text:
Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and other nations, according to a US intelligence memo addressed to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio cited by Axios. The intel also warned that plots targeting US diplomats were reaching "advanced stages"..
In the one-page memo sent to Rubio on October 23, US officials expressed concern that Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen could widen the scope of their attacks beyond Saudi Arabia to other countries in the region, Axios reported.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also warned Rubio that intelligence about the alleged assassination plots by Iran must reach more US personnel than are currently authorised to receive it.
The memo cited by Axios does not identify specific targers or countries outside Middle East, but mentions that the intelligence about Iran's plots has already been shared with senior US State Department officials.
US Orders Departure Of Non-Emergency Personnel From Saudi Arabia
Amid the security concerns, the US Department of State has ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia.
However, Department of State Spokesperson Tommy Pigott rejected reports suggesting that Washington was preparing to issue similar departure orders across multiple Gulf embassies, clarifying that the measure applied only to Saudi Arabia.
"This is inaccurate. The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," he wrote in a post on X.

Explaining the security concerns behind the decision, Pigott pointed to an increase in attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian infrastructure.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," he added.
Trump Warns Iran Of Another Possible US Strike
The latest intelligence assessment comes amid renewed warnings from US President Donald Trump, who on Friday threatened the possibility of another American military strike if Tehran fails to reach a diplomatic agreement with Washington.
Addressing a campaign rally in Florida, Trump suggested that the US could launch "another little Epic Fury" if Iran does not agree to a deal.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," Trump told the cheering crowd.

Questioning Tehran's willingness to negotiate, the US president said, "If they're smart, they'll just say, 'Let's get down to business.' But, you know, I doubt they'll do that because perhaps they're not smart," he added.
The developments come ahead of the US midterm elections, scheduled for the first week of November. Analysts believe tensions in West Asia could escalate further as Washington and Tehran continue to harden their respective positions.

news.title: Russia senator says Western sanctions may remain in place forever
news.text:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Western countries may temporarily ease sanctions against Russia in their own interests, but they are unlikely to completely abandon them, Federation Council Vice Speaker Konstantin Kosachev said in an interview with TASS.

But Moscow should not worry, because it has proven its self-sufficiency.

"It can be assumed that we will live to see the moment when sanctions are lifted legally, but, in my view, their inclusion in US legislation and in the relevant directives of the European Union is, if not an eternal phenomenon, then at least an extremely long·term one, because lifting sanctions requires consensus — a convincing majority, in case of US Congress, or consensus, unanimity, in case of the European Union," the senator said.

According to Kosachev, temporary exceptions to the sanctions regime are possible thanks to the interests of the Western countries.

"My prediction is that the sanctions regime will be eased over time, because maintaining it at its current maximum level clearly runs counter to the interests of those who came up with and are using these sanctions," he explained.

However, the parliamentarian continued, the Westerners will certainly retain the ability to reinstate the sanctions at any time if "Russia behaves, in their view, in a way they do not like."

"I am convinced that this is not the issue we should be focusing on, because over these decades -- if we look at the period starting from 2008, when sanctions related to the Georgian issue first appeared -- we have proven that Russia cannot be isolated, that Russia cannot be broken even by the most severe sanctions, and that we are able to maintain our self·sufficiency and our ability to develop regardless of what is happening around us," the senator believes.

He added that the maintenance or lifting of anti-Russian sanctions in one form or another is "a headache for those who imposed these sanctions," not for Russia.

Sanctions and Russian diesel fuel

The White House is exempting Russian diesel fuel supplies to global markets from sanctions until April 7. On October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump discussed over the phone the supply of petroleum products. Later, the Russian president confirmed Moscow’s readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak previously told TASS that Russia is beginning to lift the ban on diesel fuel exports early and is ready to supply 100,000 tons of diesel in October, 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons in December, with the potential to increase this volume to 3 million tons per month.
news.summary: Konstantin Kosachev stressed that Moscow should not worry, because it has proven its self-sufficiency
news.author: Tass

news.title: “I Want to Give Back”: Afrikaner Refugees Arrive in US With Hopes of a New Life
news.text:
Forty-two South African Afrikaners from 18 families have arrived in the United States under President Donald Trump’s refugee resettlement programme, with some expressing their desire to build new lives and contribute to their new home.

The group landed at Washington Dulles International Airport on Tuesday evening, 20 October 2026, marking the latest arrival under the programme. According to The Daily Wire, which reported on the arrivals on 21 October, the initiative has brought more than 17,000 South Africans to the US since Trump signed an executive order in February 2025.

Among the arrivals were individuals who described experiences of loss, fear and uncertainty in South Africa, while expressing hope for a fresh start in America.

Tina Burger, who arrived with her second husband, Fred, shared a deeply personal account of the tragedy that shaped her life. Her first husband, a farmer, was murdered by an unknown attacker nearly three decades ago, just one week before she gave birth.

Despite the painful experience, Burger said she wanted to focus on giving back to the country that had welcomed her and her family.

“I want to mean something. I want to give something of myself to your country to say thank you for what you are doing for me,” she told The Daily Wire.

Her remarks highlighted the desire among some of the new arrivals to contribute to American society rather than simply seek refuge.

Another refugee, who chose to remain anonymous, also spoke about his experiences in South Africa. He said he was not expecting special treatment but wanted the opportunity to live and work on an equal footing with others.

The man also revealed that he knew three people who had been murdered in South Africa in recent years, adding to the concerns he cited when discussing his decision to leave the country.

Meanwhile, a young mother among the arrivals reportedly described how fear had influenced her family’s daily life in South Africa.

She explained that her children’s activities had largely been restricted to school, church and home because of concerns about their safety. The family hoped their move to the United States would offer them greater freedom and the opportunity to experience a different way of life.

The arrivals come amid ongoing debate surrounding the Trump administration’s decision to resettle white South Africans under its refugee programme. The policy has drawn international attention, particularly over the administration’s claims about the circumstances facing Afrikaners in South Africa.

The South African government has disputed the characterisation of white Afrikaners as a group facing persecution, maintaining that the country’s challenges, including violent crime, affect people across racial and socioeconomic groups.

Nevertheless, for the 42 new arrivals, the immediate focus appears to be settling into their new surroundings and starting the next chapter of their lives.

Burger’s commitment to contribute to the United States reflects the hopes expressed by some members of the group as they begin adjusting to life in a new country.

For Burger, the move represents not only an opportunity to seek security but also a chance to give something back to the country that has opened its doors to her.

news.title: Trump unveils 'American-made' seafood label
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 24 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has announced a new labelling initiative to identify American-produced seafood, seeking to give domestic fishermen a competitive advantage over foreign suppliers amid growing concerns about imports, environmental standards and the future of the country's fishing industry. The announcement came at a Republican campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida, where Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. accused foreign seafood producers of using environmentally destructive practices and selling products in the United States under conditions that disadvantage American fishermen. Kennedy said the administration would introduce a label identifying seafood produced in the United States, allowing consumers to distinguish domestic products from imported alternatives. "And today he's announcing a label for all American made seafood that says it's American made, so Americans can make a good choice," Kennedy told supporters. Trump introduced the initiative as part of a broader effort to support the seafood industry along Florida's Gulf Coast. "Today, we're also taking historic action to support an important industry here on the shores of the Gulf of America," Trump said. He invited Kennedy to explain the measure, praising his longstanding involvement with commercial fishing communities. Kennedy said American fishermen were subject to stringent environmental and sustainability regulations that placed them at a disadvantage when competing against foreign producers operating under different standards. "Commercial fishermen in this country have the strongest environmental regulations. They have the greatest sustainability regulations but it puts them at a disadvantage to all the other fishermen in the world," he said. The Health Secretary singled out shrimp production in Vietnam and Cambodia, alleging that some foreign operators were destroying mangrove ecosystems and using chemicals that would make their products unacceptable in certain overseas markets. Kennedy claimed that some producers enclosed mangrove swamps, poisoned fish and cultivated shrimp over several seasons until the surrounding environment was destroyed. He further alleged that shrimp produced under such conditions contained high levels of antibiotics and disinfectants. "The shrimp are so loaded with antibiotics and disinfectants that no European country will take them," Kennedy said. He claimed those products were subsequently shipped to the United States, where domestic shrimp producers were forced to compete against lower-cost imports. The allegations against foreign producers were not accompanied by supporting evidence in the supplied remarks. Kennedy specifically highlighted Fort Myers and Florida's pink shrimp industry, describing the region as an important centre of American commercial fishing. He said the administration was working to rebuild fishing infrastructure and reopen markets for domestic producers. The proposed label, he suggested, would give American consumers a clearer choice when purchasing seafood. Neither Trump nor Kennedy specified when the labelling initiative would take effect, whether it would be mandatory or voluntary, or which federal agency would oversee its implementation. They also did not explain what production standards would qualify seafood for the American-made designation. Seafood labelling and country-of-origin requirements are significant trade issues because they can influence consumer preferences, market access and compliance costs.

news.title: Elon Musk has a lot to lose at US midterms as pollsters tip blue wave
news.text:
Last November, Elon Musk was looking to step away from the halls of power.

"You know, I've generally found that when I get involved in politics, it ends up badly," he told investor and YouTuber Nikhil Kamath.

"Best to avoid where possible."

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive's stint as a special government employee leading the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had ended months earlier after a string of controversies.

Mr Musk also quietly shelved plans to launch a political party, which had been announced during a short-lived feud with US President Donald Trump.

But as the country's midterm elections approach, Mr Musk is making another foray into politicking.

And with control of Congress now in reach for Democrats, the stakes for the trillionaire are higher than ever.

Trying to turn back a blue tide

With Mr Trump's approval rating at record lows, Democrats are banking on breakthrough performances at the November 3 elections.

Forecasters say the House of Representatives is all but guaranteed to flip blue, while the Senate result is, at the least, a toss-up.

Despite arguing that "they never poll us right", the president has embarked on a campaign blitz across the country.

He has also promised to pay every American adult $US5,000 (about $7,100) if Republicans retain control of Congress, reminiscent of the $US5,000 cheques cut from DOGE savings once floated in early 2025.

Mr Musk may be staying off the campaign trail, but behind the scenes, he has become the biggest known midterm donor, sinking about $US442 million into Republican groups in this election cycle.

At least $US158 million of that has gone toward a race in his home state of Texas, in which Republicans are at risk of losing a once-safe US Senate seat to Democratic candidate James Talarico.

Mr Talarico's campaign has released ads claiming Mr Musk wants to "buy his own US senator" by bankrolling Republican candidate Ken Paxton.

"So let's remind Elon: Texas is not for sale," the ads say.

Separately, Mr Musk earlier this month said he would give a SpaceX share to "every child in America" in 2027. While he did not provide details of the giveaway, Mr Trump claimed it as a victory for his Trump accounts program, through which he said the stock would be distributed. 

Dems put target on Musk's back

There is a lot at stake for Mr Musk if control of the House changes over.

Democrats have been calling for investigations into several areas of his dealings, and if they win back gavels in several congressional committees, they will have the power to follow through.

Mr Musk recently landed himself in Democrats' sights after Ukraine reported its access to the SpaceX owned Starlink and Starshield services had been restricted, affecting the country's ability to defend against Russian drone attacks. 

In response to the matter, Mr Musk said Starshield's systems were controlled by the US government.

Mr Trump and the SpaceX owner have denied responsibility, but a Wall Street Journal report cited officials and people familiar with the matter as saying Mr Musk ordered the throttled speeds.

Days prior, Mr Musk commented that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "gone too far" by striking Russian oil refineries.

US Representative Pramila Jayapal, a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, told Politico the incident raised questions about Mr Musk's power.

"What happens when one guy gets a giant contract from the government and then uses it to do something that shuts down communication in a war that has been extremely important to the United States to support Ukraine?" she said.

"There's a lot of different parts of the corruption around Musk."

Democrats on several committees have also earmarked DOGE for congressional scrutiny.

Through its 10-month lifespan, the department cut an estimated 250,000 federal jobs, allegedly accessed sensitive data, and withheld congressionally appropriated funds.

Democrats have also alleged conflicts of interest between Mr Musk and the federal government.

Republicans blocked previous attempts by Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform to subpoena Mr Musk.

"There's any number of House committees that would have jurisdiction in some respect over him," said Harry Melkonian, an honorary associate at the United States Studies Centre.

"He's a major defence contractor and NASA contractor, so his companies receive staggering amounts of federal money each year."

In June 2025, representative Jasmine Crockett, who sits on the oversight committee, vowed to "bring Elon Musk in" once Democrats regained the majority.

"And we can have him under oath, and we can have him tell us about everything that he did," she said in an appearance on MSNBC.

In response to the Politico report that Democrats were discussing possible investigations into Mr Musk, the trillionaire threatened to retaliate against congressional investigations.

"Live by the sword, die by the sword," he wrote on X.

"Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets."

Testimonies, document production

Mr Musk could be called to testify at committee hearings and required to produce documents under a congressional investigation.

"For somebody like Musk, it would be truly awful to be sitting for eight hours a day, having a panel of people just questioning everything you do," Dr Melkonian said.

"It becomes television news … and he is a businessman selling consumer products."

But refusing to cooperate would present its own problems.

"On the political side, as a major contractor, he would be reluctant to antagonise a congressional majority because his companies depend on money voted by Congress," Dr Melkonian said.

"Legally, he could be held in contempt of Congress."

The federal misdemeanour is punishable by imprisonment of up to 12 months.

If an investigation uncovers any wrongdoing, the findings can be referred to the Department of Justice for prosecution.

The US attorney would be bound to take the matter to a grand jury in Washington, DC.

Dr Melkonian said the findings could lead Congress to determine Mr Musk as unfit for further dealings with the government.

"They could say, 'We're not going to authorise any more spending [on government contracts with Musk]'. That's their ultimate power. Congress controls the dollars," he said.

"Whether or not it ever goes to a federal judge, I don't think he likes that."
news.summary: As the US midterm elections approach, Elon Musk is making an expensive foray back into politicking.

news.title: Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal  - Dominican Republic Post –
news.text:
An Argentinian federal judge has dropped a criminal investigation into President Javier Milei and his sister Karina Milei over the collapse of a cryptocurrency he promoted online.

Judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi issued the decision on Friday, according to court records, ending an inquiry into Milei’s role in the launch of the $Libra token, which crashed after a brief rally.

“The reported events do not constitute a criminal offence,” the judge said in a ruling. He also wrote that investor losses and the rise and fall in the currency’s price were insufficient to establish fraud.

In his ruling, Martinez de Giorgi said that Milei’s institutional standing could have given the launch “greater impact” when he posted about it, but that does not translate into a fraudulent scheme.

Javier Milei recommended the little-known meme coin in a post on X in February 2025. He later deleted the post and denied any link to the cryptocurrency, whose value soon plunged.

The judge also dismissed an investigation into US businessman Hayden Davis, who described himself as a “launch adviser” for the token. Davis has acknowledged that he held close to $100m after the crash and denies any wrongdoing.

“For the first time in history, a President of the Nation was investigated with complete freedom, resulting in absolute proof of his innocence,” read a post shared on X by the official presidential office.

“The question that remains is this: Who will take responsibility for having wasted Argentine taxpayers’ money and the President of the Nation’s time in a failed attempt at an institutional coup?”

Milei’s friendship with Trump

Milei is one of US President Donald Trump’s closest allies. Trump firmly backed him a year ago and has called him his “favourite president”.

Trump made clear the support hinged on a victory for Milei’s party.

“I’m with this man because his philosophy is correct,” he said ahead of a White House lunch with the Argentinian leader last year. “If he wins, we’re staying with him. And if he doesn’t win, we’re gone.”

Earlier this month, Milei urged Trump to emerge stronger from the US midterm elections, saying the vote mattered for the West as a whole.

Austerity at home

Since taking office in 2023, Milei has laid off thousands of state employees, shut ministries, cut subsidies and reduced government-funded programmes. The measures were meant to fight high inflation, which has fallen to about 2 percent a month.

Milei says his plan is working, claiming that Argentina has grown for 27 consecutive months and is expanding at four times its historical rate.

When the coin crashed, Milei said he had acted “in good faith” and accused his political rivals of trying to exploit the situation.

news.title: Trump hints at Cuba move after Iran campaign
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 24 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has suggested that Cuba could become the focus of renewed American pressure after the military campaign against Iran, raising the possibility of a US naval presence near the Caribbean island and a diplomatic role for Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida, Trump responded to a question about Cuba by linking the island's future to the ongoing American military operations against Iran. "Cuba, he wants to know what about Cuba. Give me a break. Give me a break. Don't worry, we'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran," Trump told supporters. The President then described a hypothetical scenario in which American naval vessels returning from the Middle East would pass close to Cuba. "Actually, what we're going to do with Cuba is we're going to come back from Iran," he said. "Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast, they'll raise up their hands and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal." The comments drew applause from the audience, although Trump delivered them in a light-hearted manner and did not announce any formal military operation or diplomatic initiative against Havana. His remarks nevertheless placed Cuba alongside Iran and Venezuela in a broader discussion of his administration's approach to foreign policy and American military power. Trump praised Rubio, who has been a prominent advocate of a tougher American approach towards Cuba. "He's a -- he's a great guy," Trump said. The President did not explain what agreement Rubio might seek, whether Washington had opened new negotiations with Havana or what conditions Cuba would have to meet. Nor did he indicate whether the proposed naval movement was under consideration by the Pentagon. Trump made the comments while highlighting what he described as successful American military action against Venezuela and Iran. He said that his administration had captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and brought him to the United States to face trial. "We captured and brought to justice the outlaw dictator of Venezuela, Nicolas Maduro, who is now awaiting trial," Trump said. The President also claimed that the operation in Venezuela had been completed in a single day and that the United States was subsequently working with the country to expand oil production. He used those assertions to portray his administration as willing to employ military force to achieve foreign policy objectives. Turning to Iran, Trump said American operations had severely weakened Tehran's military and nuclear capabilities. He also left open the possibility of further strikes if Iran failed to reach an agreement with Washington. The President did not explicitly connect his comments about Cuba to any proposed military campaign against the island. Cuba and the United States have experienced decades of strained relations since the Cuban Revolution of 1959. American sanctions and disagreements over political freedoms, security and regional influence have remained central issues in bilateral relations. Rubio, a Cuban-American politician from Florida, has long supported a hardline policy towards Havana. His position on Cuba has been an important part of his foreign policy record, making Trump's reference to a possible negotiating role for him politically significant.

news.title: US intelligence chief warns of advanced Iranian plots against American officials
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 24 (IANS) Iran has sharply stepped up efforts to target American officials, with some lethal plots now at an advanced stage, the top US intelligence official has warned Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as Washington pulls diplomats out of Saudi Arabia and trims staff at several other embassies in the region. In a one-page unclassified memo dated October 23, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Rubio that Iran had “substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel”, Axios reported, citing the document. The memo, copied to CIA Director John Ratcliffe, said lethal plots had “reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries”, according to Axios’s Barak Ravid, who first reported it. The memo did not name targets, the countries outside the Middle East or the nature of the plots, according to the report. The intelligence had already been shared with senior State Department officials, and Clayton offered to downgrade it so it could be shared more widely with State Department staff. A US official confirmed the memo to IANS. “When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment,” the official said. “The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region.” Earlier this week, the State Department ordered the departure of non-emergency staff from the US Embassy in Riyadh and the consulates in Jeddah and Dhahran. On Friday, staff reductions followed at the US embassies in the UAE, Lebanon, Qatar and Jordan. CNN, as cited by the Jerusalem Post, reported that cuts also extend to Bahrain and Kuwait, with diplomats describing the process as “chaotic”. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said on X that the ordered departure applied to “Saudi Arabia only”. The warning comes as President Donald Trump keeps open the option of renewed military action. Speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday, Trump said: “We may do another little Operation Epic Fury, or [the Iranians] will agree.” NBC News reported on October 21 that the US military has also been quietly reducing troop numbers at bases in the Middle East.

news.title: Hero dad Kaylub Giamanco makes heartbreaking admission after horror school shooting
news.text: A courageous father who fatally shot a school gunman has expressed his sorrow to the parents of the children he was unable to rescue. Kaylub Giamanco says he was the 'last line of defence' at Silver Rail Elementary in Oregon and, despite ultimately stopping the devastating attack, he wishes he had arrived earlier and been able to save more lives. "I want to apologise for not saving their babies, that's probably the biggest thing for me right now," Giamanco said. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome. But there were ones that I didn't save." Three children - ages 5, 8 and 11 - and a teacher were killed at the school in Bend, Oregon, last week when a former pupil, 16 year old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked a special needs classroom . Another student was left in a critical condition, while another teacher was also injured and taken to hospital. Giamanco had dropped his daughters off at the school that morning before heading off to work as usual. Several hours later, however, the 36 year old carpenter found himself passing the school once more while making his way home for lunch - it was then that he spotted an individual dressed in black and carrying a long firearm. The gunman opened fire on a pickup truck and at a person mowing the school's lawn, before scaling a fence and advancing towards the school building. Giamanco recalled that "panic fled into my brain." He seized a 40-caliber handgun from his truck's centre console and pursued the gunman while simultaneously dialling 911. After requesting emergency assistance from the dispatcher, he ended the call. "I said 'I'm sorry I have to go in. People are going to die,'" Giamanco said. As he drew nearer to the building, Giamanco recounted how he dropped to his stomach and crawled across the ground on his elbows. "That's when I started hearing children pleading for their lives," he said. "And then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster. And I told myself: 'This is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do.'". Giamanco revealed he entered the school through a shattered window. Peering into an adjacent classroom, he spotted a teacher locked in a struggle with the shooter. He described how they were both side-on to him, presenting a clear shot. "I felt like I was the last line of defense between him and the rest of the children," Giamanco said. He flung the door open, strode into the room and discharged his weapon. Police confirm another teacher hurled her phone at the attacker and wrestled with him before Giamanco fatally shot him. Both the gunman and the teacher collapsed to the floor. The teacher fled the room as the shooter reached for his shotgun. "He was scrambling for his weapon," Giamanco said. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else." Police confirmed that Giamanco was legally carrying his firearm in his vehicle, and have credited both him and the unarmed teacher who confronted the gunman with saving numerous lives. The day after the shooting, President Donald Trump praised Giamanco as a "great hero" who "took care of business." A second teacher present in the classroom, Becky Drury, revealed in a statement on Wednesday that she lay on the floor helplessly playing dead, after being struck at close range by a shotgun blast that nearly severed her left hand. The teacher who wrestled with the shooter has not been publicly named. Giamanco told the public broadcaster that she's "a real true hero" whose bravery gave him the opportunity to neutralise the attacker. "I can't tell you what it feels like to take a life ... but I can tell you that I genuinely feel like I was supposed to be there," Giamanco said. "If I wasn't there, I just don't know what would have happened."
news.summary: Kaylub Giamanco says he was the 'last line of defence' at Silver Rail Elementary in Oregon and, despite ultimately foiling the horrific attack, he regrets not arriving sooner and saving more lives
news.author: Peter Hennessy

news.title: Michigan Senate rivals clash over Muslim Brotherhood allegations as Rogers doubles down on El-Sayed
news.text: Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed accused Republican rival Mike Rogers of questioning his loyalty to the United States during a heated Fox News interview Friday, while Rogers doubled down on allegations that his opponent has embraced the ideology of the Muslim Brotherhood. The candidates both spoke separately with Fox News chief political anchor Bret Baier on "Special Report" in Detroit, 11 days before the Nov. 3 election. Baier pressed El-Sayed about a 2012 statement involving former Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who was affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood. EL-SAYED, ROGERS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD, TRUMP AND GUNS: 5 FIERY DEBATE MOMENTS "No, no, no, let me just stop there," El-Sayed interrupted. ABDUL EL-SAYED GROWS AGITATED WITH REPORTER AFTER BEING PRESSED ON FAMILY'S ALLEGED MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES "I'm asking a question," Baier replied. "Be a journalist," El-Sayed shot back. "I am," Baier responded. El-Sayed accused Rogers of making his Muslim faith a campaign issue, calling the suggestion "sad" and "beneath him." EL-SAYED'S PAST MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD COMMENTS RAISE RED FLAGS AS HE EYES POWERFUL ROLE The controversy centers partly on a 2012 letter that The Washington Free Beacon reported El-Sayed signed supporting decisions by then-Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, including calls to purge Egypt's police and media. El-Sayed has also faced scrutiny over social media posts from his half-sister describing their mother's alleged involvement in Muslim Brotherhood activism in the 1970s. He has denied personal or family ties to the organization and said he was raised by his father and stepmother. In an Oct. 17 Fox News interview, El-Sayed acknowledged that his sister-in-law was a plaintiff in a lawsuit challenging her alleged placement on a terrorist watchlist but insisted she had done nothing wrong. The FBI declined to confirm or deny her watchlist status. The lawsuit does not establish wrongdoing. Rogers rejected El-Sayed's characterization in his own interview. ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYED’S ‘EXTREME’ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION "I wore the uniform of the United States. Many in my family, including our son, wore the uniform of the United States so he can pray any way he wants," Rogers said. "It is not how he prays, it's how he thinks." Rogers accused El-Sayed of embracing the organization's ideology and portraying himself as a victim. "He has adopted the ideology of the Muslim Brotherhood," Rogers alleged. Baier noted that El-Sayed had denied ever belonging to the organization and pledged allegiance to the Constitution. "Does he disavow? Does he really say it?" Rogers responded. El-Sayed had explicitly disavowed the organization at an Oct. 17 town hall, answering, "Sure. Yeah, absolutely" when asked. The candidates also differed over the war with Iran, which El-Sayed blamed for rising gasoline and grocery prices. "We need a war powers resolution to end the capacity for this president to wage an illegal, unjustifiable war," El-Sayed said. Rogers defended the original rationale for military action but said he has urged President Donald Trump to end the conflict. "I've called for him to wrap it up. That's the right thing to do," Rogers said. Turning to Michigan's economy, Rogers said the state has lost 27,000 manufacturing jobs and faces some of the nation's highest auto insurance costs. He also raised concerns about education, claiming roughly two-thirds of fourth graders cannot read at grade level. Rogers defended Trump's influence in Michigan, pointing to his support among voters and crediting his trade policies with encouraging General Motors to bring Silverado pickup truck production back to the state. But the Republican acknowledged a disagreement with Trump over trade with Canada. "I've come out and said we shouldn't be doing the Canadian tariffs the way we are doing them," Rogers said. Baier also pressed El-Sayed over Medicare-for-all, and whether middle-class taxes would rise. "I'm fine with people keeping their private insurance if that's what they want, but I want guaranteed public insurance for everybody," El-Sayed said. Rogers disputed El-Sayed's position, arguing that Medicare-for-all would eliminate private insurance and raise costs for Michigan families. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP El-Sayed touted upcoming campaign appearances with former President Barack Obama and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., while questioning whether Trump would help Rogers in Michigan. With both Trump and Obama expected to campaign in Michigan over the weekend, the candidates are turning to their parties' most recognizable figures as they make their final pitches to voters ahead of Election Day.Fox News Digital's Leo Briceno contributed to this reporting.
news.summary: The Michigan Senate race heated up on "Special Report" as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers clashed over war powers, Medicare-for-all and Muslim Brotherhood allegations.

news.title: "Don't Play With Fire": Iran Warns Of Undersea Cable Attacks If War Resumes
news.text: Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections."If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.'STRONGER RESPONSE'The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's ​leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region."Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.

news.title: Trump warns of fresh military strikes on Iran
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 24 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has warned that American forces could launch another round of military strikes against Iran if Tehran fails to reach an agreement with Washington, signalling that further military action remains an option despite his claims that Iran has already suffered a decisive defeat. Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida, Trump suggested that the United States could repeat elements of its military campaign against Iran if diplomatic efforts failed to produce an agreement. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree. If they're smart, they'll just say, let's get down to business," Trump told supporters. The remarks came as the President sought to portray the military campaign as successful while keeping pressure on Tehran to accept an agreement that would prevent it from developing nuclear weapons. Trump referred to two American military operations against Iran, Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury, claiming they had destroyed the country's nuclear enrichment capabilities and severely weakened its military and economy. "We obliterated Iran's nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer," he said. The President said subsequent operations had reinforced the initial strikes. He did not outline the conditions Iran would have to meet to prevent another round of military action. "We defeated them militarily, financially and otherwise and now we are ensuring it's done," Trump said. His comments suggested that Washington was prepared to maintain military pressure even as the administration considered the possibility of an agreement. In a separate interview with Florida television station WINK-TV, Trump offered a similar assessment of how the conflict might end. "I see it ending soon. I see it ending one way or another, through agreement or otherwise," he said. The President did not provide a timetable for ending the conflict or specify whether negotiations were underway. Trump maintained that preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons remained the overriding objective of American military operations. He argued that earlier administrations had failed to address the threat and said he had faced a difficult decision because of the potential consequences of military action. "I had to attack Iran, or they would have had a nuclear weapon," Trump said during the television interview. He also defended the use of B-2 bombers in the campaign, claiming that Iran would otherwise have acquired a nuclear weapon. At the Fort Myers rally, Trump also described the economic pressure facing Iran, claiming that the country was experiencing severe inflation and financial difficulties. He said American military and economic measures had left Tehran with little choice but to reconsider its position. The President linked the military campaign to American naval operations around the Strait of Hormuz, claiming that the US Navy was enforcing a blockade against Iran while allowing other shipping to pass. He said oil shipments through the strategic waterway had increased despite the conflict.

news.text: A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to ensure a senior Interior Department official preserves his personal phone’s contents, marking a new development in an increasingly contentious legal battle over the president’s plans to overhaul a historic golf course in Washington, D.C. In a minute order, obtained by Newsweek, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes directed the government to ensure that Gregory Wischer, the Interior's deputy chief of staff for policy, had taken “appropriate steps” to preserve the contents of his phone. Reyes also expanded an existing preservation requirement covering text messages related to the litigation to include “any material concerning the East Potomac Golf Course and this litigation.” The judge added that the order “should be broadly construed.” Wischer has played a central role in the administration's handling of the course. He testified during an October 19 hearing about the development of the tree-removal plan and the administration's proposed redesign, telling the hearing he had learned of President Donald Trump's announced November 15 closure date through the president's social media post. He also testified that a new golf-course design had been sent to his personal phone. The preservation order does not specify that the phone itself must be surrendered to the court or that its contents must immediately be turned over to the plaintiffs. Its stated requirement is that the government ensure appropriate preservation steps have been taken. The ruling is the latest development in the dispute over Trump's proposed transformation of East Potomac Golf Links, a public course on federal land managed by the National Park Service. The lawsuit challenges the administration's handling of tree removal and its compliance with federal environmental-review requirements. Reyes denied the plaintiffs' request to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO), which bars additional tree cutting through Monday, and denied without prejudice their motion to resume testimony. The motion notes the plaintiffs—the D.C. Preservation League and local golfers Alex Dickson and Dave Roberts—may renew their request ahead of a permanent-injunction hearing, though Reyes has not announced a date for further proceedings or indicated whether she will grant longer-term relief. East Potomac Golf Legal Battle Timeline 2025: Interior Department Terminates Public Golf Course Operator's Lease The Interior Department terminated National Links Trust's lease to operate three public golf courses in Washington, including East Potomac Golf Links. The nonprofit continued operating East Potomac and Langston Golf Course under an interim arrangement. The move helped clear the way for the Trump administration to take control of the properties and fueled concerns among local golfers that the courses could be transformed in ways that would limit affordable public access. February 13, 2026: Golfers and Preservation Group Sue Trump Administration The D.C. Preservation League and two frequent East Potomac golfers, Roberts and Dickson, sued the Interior and National Park Service in federal court. The lawsuit challenged the administration's broader plans for the course, alleging violations of federal environmental, historic-preservation and administrative-procedure requirements. The plaintiffs also raised concerns about debris from the demolition of the White House's East Wing being brought to East Potomac Park. At the time, the administration had not publicly released a detailed design, but Trump had already discussed turning East Potomac into a championship-level golf course. The plaintiffs sought to block the project and challenge the government's actions before further changes could be made. Spring 2026: Lawsuit Proceeds as Administration Defends Its Plans The government challenged the lawsuit, arguing in part that no final agency action had occurred that could be reviewed by the court. It maintained that the proposed redevelopment remained conceptual. The court held hearings on the parties' competing motions. Reyes initially declined to impose an injunction, relying instead on government assurances that officials would notify the plaintiffs and the court of major developments beyond ordinary maintenance. May 2026: Administration Unveils Initial Golf Course Design Interior Secretary Doug Burgum publicly unveiled a design for an 18-hole championship course, a nine-hole short course and expanded practice facilities. The announcement gave the redevelopment proposal greater definition, although the administration continued to argue in court that the project had not reached the stage of final agency action. June 28, 2026: Trump Announces Work Will Begin September 1 After visiting East Potomac Golf Links with golf-course architect Tom Fazio and Interior officials, Trump announced on Truth Social that the administration would build one of the world's greatest golf courses, with work scheduled to begin September 1. The plaintiffs viewed the announcement as evidence that the project was advancing despite the government's earlier descriptions of the plans as conceptual. The administration continued to dispute the plaintiffs' characterization. July-September 2026: Judge Relies on Government Assurances During proceedings in July and September, the government continued to maintain that the project had not reached the stage requiring the court to intervene. Reyes agreed to rely on assurances that officials would notify the plaintiffs and the court of major developments involving the course outside ordinary maintenance. Those assurances became central to the dispute after the government moved ahead with tree removal in October. October 5-6, 2026: Officials Develop and Approve Tree-Removal Plan According to Reyes' October 13 opinion, Wischer directed officials on October 5 to implement recommendations from a 2019 National Park Service cultural-landscape report “as soon as practical.” Acting National Park Service Director Jessica Bowron approved the tree-management plan the following day. The government later argued that the work was intended to restore the course's historic landscape, rather than implement Trump's broader redesign. Reyes questioned why officials had moved so quickly on a plan based on an older report, particularly when the government had previously described the redevelopment as conceptual and had agreed to provide notice of major changes. October 9-10, 2026: Hundreds of Trees Removed The government notified the court late October 9 that the National Park Service planned to remove up to 529 trees beginning the next morning. By the end of October 10, crews had removed approximately 430 healthy non-invasive trees, according to Reyes' opinion. The judge wrote that hundreds more might have been removed but for a rain delay. The plaintiffs argued that the tree removal was part of the larger redevelopment and that the administration had proceeded without the required environmental review. The government maintained that the work was separate maintenance based on the 2019 landscape report. October 12-13, 2026: Judge Issues Temporary Restraining Order At an emergency hearing on October 12, Reyes sharply questioned government attorneys about the timing of the tree removal and whether it was connected to Trump's proposed redesign. In an opinion issued October 13, Reyes granted the plaintiffs' request for a TRO barring further tree removal through October 26. She found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that the government had failed to comply with federal environmental-review requirements. The order also required advance notice before certain additional irreversible changes to the course. October 16-19, 2026: DOJ Seeks Judge's Removal as Trump Publicizes New Plans The Justice Department filed a motion seeking Reyes' recusal, accusing her of bias and "improper "open hostility" toward government attorneys. Reyes rejected the request on October 18. Over the same weekend, Trump publicized an updated course design and announced that East Potomac Golf Links would close November 15 for approximately 15 months of renovation. The updated proposal differed from the earlier design and intensified questions about whether the administration's plans had moved beyond the conceptual stage. Trump also launched a personal attack on Reyes, writing on Truth Social, “The judge on the case is a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane?” October 19, 2026: Senior Officials Testify in Court Reyes held a lengthy hearing at which Wischer and Bowron were questioned about the tree-removal plan, the administration's decision-making and the status of the proposed redevelopment. The judge pressed officials on the relationship between the tree removal and Trump's public announcements. The hearing ended without a final ruling on longer-term injunctive relief. October 22, 2026: Judge Orders Phone Preservation but Denies TRO Extension Reyes ordered the government to ensure that Wischer had taken appropriate steps to preserve the contents of his personal phone. In the same minute order, Reyes denied the plaintiffs' motion to extend the TRO and denied without prejudice their request to resume testimony. The existing TRO is set to expire Monday unless the court takes further action. Reyes has not indicated in that order whether she will issue a preliminary injunction or what restrictions any future order might impose. What Happens Next The immediate question is whether Reyes will issue further restrictions before the TRO expires on Monday. Any preliminary injunction would establish the restrictions that remain in effect while the litigation continues. Its scope could determine whether additional tree removal or other irreversible work can proceed before the court resolves the plaintiffs' claims. news.summary: A judge has ordered a Trump official to preserve his personal phone’s contents in the latest update in a golf course legal battle.
